# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Borrowing a pair to try under stage lights or on a noisy walk sits naturally with trying one first, and the audience questions and eleven people at lunch both come down to many voices at once, though a family lunch is hardly a big room; Diego's cost worry fits neither group and stays on its own rightly.
whys.g2: Tomás's answer about sitting on his good side doesn't say what would make it worth more, and it was kept out of the groups, so nothing off-topic got grouped.

founder.order_why: Who decides (screen 10) and who else has to agree (screen 14, with its checks at 15 and 16) belong together, but the cost and price questions (12 and 13) sit between them, so I answered the buying question in two halves.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14 both ask whether anyone besides the wearer decides or pays; for AirCaps I gave the same answer twice (the wearer, nobody else). Screens 3 and 4 also carry the same kicker and question.
founder.missing: There was no way to give a one-off hardware price next to a subscription: AirCaps is $599 glasses up front plus an optional $20/month Pro plan, and I had to fold that into a yearly range ($599 to $839). Nothing asked whether HSA/FSA funds pay part of it, and that changes who really pays.

PRIMARY.order_why: It jumps from one question about how often I lose the thread straight to a price, the counter skips from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5 with a 'One more thing' squeezed in, and I'm never asked what I use today before being asked what AirCaps is worth.
PRIMARY.missing: What I do today when a conversation is too fast or noisy (a phone captioning app, my hearing aids, lipreading, asking people to repeat, bringing an interpreter) and what that costs me; where it happens most, like restaurants, work meetings or the theatre; and whether I'd actually wear glasses all day.

screens.why7: The box asks for one step of up to 9 words that the people take and where the money goes, as the card's founder step requires, and the chip is the founder-side way to leave the dimension out.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take, in up to 9 words (e.g. 'order a pair with free returns' or 'try the free captions app'), and does it cost them money?

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first step and its cost, checking how Keel wrote it for strangers is the obvious next screen.
screens.why2: "Order a pair with free returns" reads fine to me, but a stranger who is deaf or hard of hearing will ask "a pair of what?" because the glasses have dropped out of the wording.
screens.why3: Ordering glasses with a return window is a step I know my wearers take; they buy hearing tech this way, often with HSA/FSA money.
screens.why4: There are two rows, the step and a smaller step at 6 and 7 words, which is the right shape, but the step leaves out what is being ordered, and the screen shows only word counts for the smaller step, so I cannot check its words.
screens.why5: Free returns is kept, but "glasses" is lost, so the belief no longer names my product's form, which drifts a little from what I meant.
screens.why7: The step costs money, so a smaller step is correctly carried and the belief can be supported or refuted at the 1-in-3 bar, but the card wants the step to name what it acts on, and dropping "glasses" is a pitfall the card lists by name, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Step: "order the caption glasses with free returns" (7 words); smaller step: "a free try of the captions on your phone"; belief: Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order the caption glasses with free returns.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, it makes sense to decide whether strangers who are keen get a way to raise their hand, and I've already named my first real step on the screens before.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is plain to me as a founder, and the hint spells out exactly what the respondent will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect emails from deaf and hard-of-hearing people who'd try AirCaps is entirely my own call to make.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The answer stores my step 'order a pair with free returns', but neither this screen nor the respondent's line shows it; the line is a generic 'try this for real', which is vaguer than my actual ask of ordering a $599 pair with 15-day returns.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order a pair with free returns? Leave your email." -- Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before strangers see the study, after the pilot offer and before the link goes out.
screens.why2: It's a plain choice between two named voices with a preview, and the hint says clearly what the 400 credits buy and that the link goes by text message.
screens.why3: I can hear both voices and pick, and I know whether my people would rather read than listen.
screens.why4: For deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents the option I'd most want, a text-only interviewer with no spoken voice (or the face kept steady and well lit for lipreading), is missing; the hint only says reading is allowed alongside the voice.
screens.why5: It still says 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' as I typed it, and nothing of AirCaps or the glasses leaks to the respondent through the voice choice.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Daphne (voice + face, captions on screen) / Saskia (voice + face, captions on screen) / Text only, no voice: the questions written on screen to read and tap

screens.why1: Choosing how my respondents answer belongs right after choosing who asks them, just before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Read and tap, an AI interviewer and let them choose are plain words to me, and each option says what the respondent does.
screens.why3: I know how my deaf and hard-of-hearing users take in a conversation, so I can pick the format that suits them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the field, but for a deaf audience the AI option leads with asking aloud, and no option lets a Deaf ASL user answer in sign.
screens.why5: My pick of Read and tap stands as typed, and nothing of AirCaps leaks into how respondents answer.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or speak into boxes) / AI interviewer on video with every question captioned on screen / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three options are plain to me, though 'the Contacts page' assumes I have already seen that part of Keel.
screens.why3: I know who I would send this to: hard-of-hearing people I've met through TranscribeGlass and AirCaps by name, or one link posted in an HLAA chapter or Deaf community group.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and one open link in a group are distinct and cover how I would actually reach people, and I can use more than one if I need to.
screens.why5: Nothing about AirCaps or the wearer role is changed or shown to respondents; this screen is only about where my links go.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right under the title with the deciding count, 1 of 7 losing 12 or more conversations a month, beside it, and the 'worst of all its cards' rule explains why Existing sacrifice names it.
screens.why_b2: Each card says what is counted (lose 12+ conversations, valued at $599+, decided alone), over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), so I read every line on first look, though the numbering jumps from 4 to 6 with no word on what 5 was.
screens.why_b3: Price, Buyer and payer and Commitment are my beliefs, but my Existing sacrifice was $200 to $1,500 a year that people already spend on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, and here it is restated as about 12 lost conversations a month, which I recognise as the pain but not as the money belief I typed.
screens.why_b4: 'They value it below your price' and 'they lose less today than you estimated' tell me what failed, but nothing says what to do, such as testing a lower up-front price or the free-captions tier, or finding the wearers who already pay for captions, and the statement under the verdict is about interview design, not my next step.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible everywhere and nothing is called strong, but no line says seven is a small sample, and 'Holding up' on Commitment rests on six stated yeses to a free-returns order, not on orders.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 1 of 7 at or above the low against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Seven cells and the 2-in-3 bar are clear, but the unit reads 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month', and a marker at 5 on a 0-to-15 conversations axis makes me stop and work out whether 5 is a count of people or of conversations.
screens.why_b3: My Existing sacrifice was money, $200 to $1,500 a year on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, and this card tests 'about 12 conversations a month', a count I never typed, worded as a garbled loss line.
screens.why_b4: 'The Price card, next, says what they would pay regardless' points me onward but does not say what a low count means for my cost estimate or for Ability to pay.
screens.why_b5: 'They lose less today than you estimated' calls my estimate wrong, but I estimated dollars a year, not conversations a month, so seven answers in another unit cannot overturn it, even with the honest 'a lean, not a call'.
screens.instead: Ask what they spent last year on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, in dollars, and read it against my $200 to $1,500 a year; or, if this card stays on conversations, say plainly that it does not test my money estimate.

screens.why_b1: Not holding up sits right beside 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front and 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Both ladders show each band's count marked for or against, my $599 and $20 sit on a band's low edge, and the 5-of-7 bar is under each, so I see seven people, nobody at my price, and where the bar is.
screens.why_b3: Price, and $599 up front then an optional $20 a month plan, is what I charge and what my site says.
screens.why_b4: It says most people chose $250 to under $599 and sends me to Insights, but it never says what to do, such as test a lower entry price or lead with a borrow or demo pair. Three of the quotes ask for exactly that, and I already offer 15-day returns.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, it calls itself a lean and not a call, and it claims nothing beyond the seven answers.
screens.instead: Nobody of 7 would pay $599 up front; six put it at $250 to under $599 and three asked to try a pair first, so test a lower entry price and lead with the 15-day free returns before reading this as a no.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Not reached' sits right beside its deciding number, 0 of 7 named your price or more, so I know this card decides nothing and why.
screens.why_b2: Three bars all at 0 say plainly nobody was asked, but the strip draws 5 ghost cells for 7 people and shows no bar marker, so I need a second look to square it with 'not asked: 7 named less'.
screens.why_b3: The belief is one Keel derived (I typed no ability-to-pay line), and it says $599 up front plus an optional $20 a month rather than my $599 to $839 a year, so I recognise it but it is not word for word mine.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until at least 5 do' tells me the card is blocked behind Price, but not what to do: test a lower entry price, or lean on HSA/FSA eligibility.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the 7, keeps n visible, says outright that nobody was asked, and lists each person's lower price band.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of 7 named $599 or more (6 said $250 to under $599), so nobody was asked where the money would come from. Fix Price first; a price near $499 would put most of them in reach.

screens.why_b1: Holding up is stated with 6 of 7 decided alone and the bar of 5 of 7 right beside it, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who had to agree over 7 people, the bar sits at 5 of 7 (at least 2 in 3), and the strip shows 6 for and 1 against at a glance.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, with the wearer deciding and nobody else agreeing, is what I picked; the bar line puts it as I said it, nobody else has to agree.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count; it doesn't tell me I can sell straight to the wearer without winning over a spouse, child or audiologist, or that with price at 0 of 7 the problem is what they'll pay, not who signs off.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible and the count line says a small group is a lean, not a call, so the flat 'they decide alone' is qualified on the same screen.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean on 7: 6 decided on their own, so you can sell to the wearer directly; who pays isn't your obstacle, the price is.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7', so I know the belief held and by what margin.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip puts my bar at 5 with its rule spelled out, so I take it in at once.
screens.why_b3: It is my step, word for word: 'order a pair with free returns', under Commitment.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is a generic call-to-action. Nobody is 'booked into' ordering glasses, and three cards back the Price card said 0 of 7 value it at $599. A yes to ordering with free returns is not a yes to keeping a pair at that price, and this card does not say what to do about that.
screens.why_b5: The small group is called a lean, which is honest. But the rule line counts 'probably, after a free look at a working pair first' while the chart's soft yes reads 'Probably yes', so I cannot tell which second option people were actually served. The 'Asked: Asked:' doubling adds noise.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean: 6 of 7 would order a pair with free returns, but on the Price card none valued it at $599, so expect returns. Next, ask these six what they would keep a pair for.

screens.why_b1: Not holding up sits right beside 0 of 7 at $599 or more and 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: The line is Price and the belief is my own: $599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what this means for AirCaps; I have to work out for myself that the trial theme points at leading with the 15-day returns, and that most answers cluster at $250 to under $599.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible (7 against, 6 asked here, Amaka never saw it), and nothing is claimed beyond those seven people.
screens.why_b6: I learn three things I did not type: people want to try a pair in their own hard setting before paying, which my free returns are clearly not getting across; they value catching many voices in a big room; and some get by for free with seating and lipreading, so 'On their own' is the free alternative I am competing with.
screens.instead: Say it outright: most valued the glasses at $250 to under $599 and wanted to try them in their own noisy setting first, so lead with the 15-day free trial and test a lower entry price.

screens.why1: As the first screen, a screener that checks whether I'm among the people this study is for makes obvious sense.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how deaf people talk about everyone else, so the question is plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I know without guessing that I deal with hearing people at work, in shops and with family every week.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate, and no escape is the right call for a screener.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment in my own community's words and gives away nothing of any product.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says well aloud, though by §17 the voice should close with "Yes or no." rather than the bare stem.

screens.why1: After being asked whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to be shown the idea before I'm asked what I think of it.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses, the lens and eye contact are all words I use about my own conversations, so I get it on first reading.
screens.why3: Missing what people say in a fast or noisy chat, and looking down at a phone for captions instead of at the person, is exactly my week.
screens.why4: This is a card to read, with no options on it.
screens.why5: The product is named on purpose as an idea to imagine, and it is described plainly without any of the company's own labels for people like me.
screens.why6: It is four short sentences I can follow by ear, though 'lightweight glasses' is said twice in a row.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions of nearby speech. While people near you talk, the captions of what they say appear inside the lens. The people building it believe you could read the words and still keep eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the weekly-conversations gate, it makes sense to ask how often this already happens to me.
screens.why2: 'Go without the thread' isn't how I'd put it; I'd say I lost track or couldn't follow, so I had to read it twice to be sure that's what it meant.
screens.why3: It's my own life, but I talk with hearing people almost every day, so a count for a whole month would be a rough guess, not something I remember.
screens.why4: A number box labelled 'conversations last month', with None and I can't recall kept apart, covers every answer I could give without overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but 'going without the thread' has drifted from conversations that are too fast or too noisy to follow into an idiom the founder likely didn't type.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, one box and one spoken escape, though the idiom is harder to catch by ear than on the page.
screens.why7: The box keeps one measure (conversations a month) and the escape is right, but the verb is the vague kind the card warns about: 'go without the thread' doesn't name what I saw go, which was being able to follow.
screens.instead: Last month, in about how many conversations with hearing people could you not follow what was being said? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after the AirCaps card and the question about how often I lose the thread, it makes sense to ask what the glasses would be worth to me, and I'm the one who'd pay for them myself.
screens.why2: Up front and then a month is how I already think about hearing gear and caption apps, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I've priced hearing aids, captioning apps and streamers out of my own pocket, so I know what I'd put down for glasses and a subscription.
screens.why4: Both ladders run cleanly with no amount in two places, 'I wouldn't pay for this' is a real answer I might give, and 'I can't say' sits apart as the one way out.
screens.why5: The only AirCaps words I meet are the idea card shown on purpose, and nothing about the company's plans or its words for people like me slips in.
screens.why6: Each step is one short question with four options and then a pick of two, which I could follow on the phone, especially with the option card on screen in the same order.
screens.why7: One price first then a plan gets two six-rung ladders on the one measure (dollars up front, dollars a month), each with a band edge at what looks like the founder's low ($599, $20), two bands below plus 'I wouldn't pay' against and three bands for, and 'I can't say' as the only escape.

screens.why1: Straight after I put a price on AirCaps, it makes sense to ask what would make me pay more for it.
screens.why2: It plays back my answer as about $250 to $600 up front, the way I'd say it, and 'worth more' is plain.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would make it worth more to me: captions that keep up in a noisy pub or at a family dinner where everyone talks over each other.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It names AirCaps, which I met on the idea card, and nothing else of the founder's plan or their words for people comes through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences with one question, and the dollar range says easily aloud.

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on AirCaps, asking whether I'd have needed anyone's say-so to buy something like it follows naturally, though the counter jumping from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5 is a small jolt.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself, and I could answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I know who had a say the last time I bought hearing tech or a captioning app (just me, or my partner, or the audiologist and insurance), so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone to someone else's decision, none overlap, and I can't say fits as the way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of the company's plan or its own terms for people reaches me; it just asks who had to agree.
screens.why6: It is one short question and a list of four short options I can hold by ear, then one escape; the spoken first option says You decided where the screen says I decided, which sounds fine aloud but is not word for word.
screens.why7: Nobody else is tested in the past form, the four are in order with Someone else had to agree second, only I decided on my own counts for, the other three count against, and the one escape I can't say is apart.

screens.why1: After asking what AirCaps would be worth to me and who else would have to agree, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the obvious next step, though the 'What you do today' kicker sits oddly over a would-you question.
screens.why2: 'Order a pair with free returns' is how I'd say it myself, and the card above says it's glasses, so 'a pair' is clear on first read and first hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd send off for a pair of caption glasses I could return, since I've weighed captioning gadgets against getting back to the theatre before.
screens.why4: Four distinct answers from a firm yes to a flat no, in my words, with the hesitant yes and the hesitant no both there and nothing missing.
screens.why5: The step reads as the founder wrote it, with 'free returns' kept, and nothing of their plan or their own terms for people reaches me beyond the idea card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options spoken as a list I can hold: yes you'd order a pair with free returns, probably yes, probably not, or no.
screens.why7: The first option is a yes to the founder's own step, 'Probably yes' is a soft yes to the same step, there are two for and two against with No as the floor and no escape, so the belief can be both held and refuted.
